His face was deeply sunburned and more than half covered by whiskers and a moustache. He carried a huge oak club but seemed to have no other weapon. He bowed awkwardly and wished us good evening in French. His accent had something of Neufchatel about it, but still clearly suggested that he came from Paris.

"Sit down, my friend," Dupin said. "I imagine you've come about the orangutan. I must say, I almost envy you for owning him. He's a magnificent animal and surely very valuable. How old do you think he is?"

The sailor took a deep breath, looking like a man suddenly freed from an unbearable burden. Then he answered confidently:

"I can't tell for certain, but he can't be older than four or five. Have you got him here?"

"Oh no. We have nowhere suitable to keep him. He's at a stable in nearby Rue Dubourg. You can collect him in the morning. Of course, you can prove he's yours?"

"Certainly I can, sir."

"I'll be sorry to lose him," Dupin said.

"I don't expect you to have gone to all this trouble for nothing, sir," the man replied. "That wouldn't be fair. I'm quite willing to pay a reward for finding him—anything reasonable, that is."

"Well," my friend said, "that's perfectly fair. Let me think. What shall I ask for? Ah, I know. This will be my reward: tell me everything you know about the murders in the Rue Morgue."

Dupin spoke the final words very softly and calmly. Just as calmly, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he took a pistol from inside his coat and placed it on the table without the least sign of agitation.

The sailor's face reddened as though he were choking. He sprang up and seized his club, but a moment later he sank back into his chair, shaking violently and looking as pale as death. He said nothing. I felt deeply sorry for him.

"My friend," Dupin said kindly, "you're frightening yourself without reason. Truly, you are. We mean you no harm at all. I give you my word as a gentleman and a Frenchman that we have no intention of hurting you. I know perfectly well that you did not commit those terrible crimes in the Rue Morgue. But you cannot deny that you were involved in them to some extent.

The storm raged violently throughout the night, but nothing particularly noteworthy happened. In the morning, however, the family came down to breakfast and discovered the dreadful bloodstain on the floor again. 'I can't believe Paragon Detergent is to blame,' Washington said. 'I've tried it on everything. It must be the ghost.' He scrubbed the stain away once more, but it returned the following morning. It was there on the third morning too, despite Mr. Otis personally locking the library overnight and taking the key upstairs. Now everyone was intrigued. Mr. Otis began to suspect he had been too categorical in denying the existence of ghosts. Mrs. Otis declared her intention to join the Psychical Society, while Washington drafted a lengthy letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore on the Persistence of Bloodstains Associated with Crime. That night, all doubt about the actual existence of supernatural apparitions disappeared forever.

The weather had been warm and sunny, and in the cool of the evening the family went for a drive. They returned at nine and had a light supper. Ghosts never entered the conversation, so even the initial state of expectant receptiveness that so often precedes psychic manifestations was absent. As Mr. Otis later informed me, they discussed only the usual subjects of cultivated, upper-class Americans: Miss Fanny Davenport's overwhelming superiority to Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; the difficulty of finding sweetcorn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy even in the best English homes; Boston's contribution to the development of the world-soul; the convenience of checking luggage when travelling by train; and the sweetness of a New York accent compared with a London drawl. The supernatural went entirely unmentioned, and nobody referred to Sir Simon de Canterville in any way. The family went to bed at eleven, and by half past eleven the house was dark. Some time later, an unusual sound in the corridor outside his bedroom woke Mr. Otis. It resembled the clanking of metal and seemed to approach with every moment. He immediately rose, struck a match, and checked the time: exactly one o'clock. He was perfectly composed and felt his pulse, which showed no trace of fever. The strange sound persisted, now accompanied by clearly audible footsteps. He put on his slippers, removed a small oblong vial from his dressing case, and opened the door.

Knights and horses wearing heavy armour could not move very quickly. These men would travel as fast as they could, and with the ground firm and free of snow or mud, they would probably manage seven miles an hour. They would need to change horses a couple of times and should arrive around six, perhaps a little later. There would still be plenty of daylight. They would recognize the white cloth I planned to tie around my right arm, and I would take command. We would surround the prison and rescue the king in no time. Altogether it would make a splendid, colourful scene, though I would have preferred noon for a more dramatic effect.

To give myself another chance of success, I decided to find some people I had recognized earlier and tell them who I was. That might get us out of trouble without waiting for the knights. But I needed to be careful; it was a risky plan. I had to acquire magnificent clothes, and I couldn't simply rush out and put them on. I needed to build up gradually, buying one outfit after another at shops far apart. Each outfit would be a little finer than the last, until I reached silk and velvet and was ready to act. So I set off.

The scheme collapsed almost at once! At the first corner I ran straight into one of our slaves, prowling about with a watchman. I happened to cough, and he shot me a look that chilled me to the bone. I guessed he recognized the sound. I immediately entered a shop and moved down the counter, asking prices while watching from the corner of my eye. The two men had stopped outside and were talking and looking through the door. I decided to escape through the back, if there was a way out. I asked the shopwoman whether I could go behind the shop to search for the escaped slave, who was thought to be hiding somewhere there. I told her I was an officer in disguise. My partner, I said, was at the door guarding one of the murderers. Would she kindly tell him not to wait, but to go straight to the far end of the back alley and stand ready to catch the fugitive when I drove him out?

She was burning with curiosity to see one of the murderers who were already so famous, and immediately hurried off to deliver the message.
